svg.title: State bytes against history: attention against the scan
svg.desc: Persistent sequence state at f64 for history lengths 16, 64, 256, and 1,024 tokens: attention keeps a key and a value row per token and grows linearly; the state-space scan keeps one 32-value state whatever the history. The table beside the curves gives the measured prefill microseconds per token of each block on the same fresh input, honest about the sequential scan's interpreter cost.
svg.text: STATE BYTES AGAINST HISTORY -- what sequence memory costs
WHAT: bytes a decoder must keep per sequence (D, from shapes) and microseconds per token of prefill (M, this machine).
bytes, log scale: pink = attention rows, blue = scan state
one fresh [history, 16] input, mean of three forwards
bytes are D: 2 x history x 16 x 8 (attention), 32 x 8 (scan)
WHY: on a CPU with little RAM the memory that grows with the conversation is the key-value cache; a fixed state removes
that growth. The price at this scale is a sequential scan: one interpreter step per position, so its microseconds per
token do not fall with batching the way one matmul over the window does. Both numbers are stated, not one.
HOW: u:kv_bytes and u:ssm_state_bytes in lib/ssm.mlpl; u:us_per_token times causal_attention against u:ssm_out on randn input.
Just ssm write re-measures and re-pins the fixture; check mode reads the pinned microseconds and re-derives the bytes.
